headline: Atsumeru is from Old Japanese 集む (atumu).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 集む (atumu), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Mittomonai is a vowel shortening and gemination of みとうもない (mitōmonai), from みたくもない (mitakumonai, “don't even want to see”).

sources.quote: Vowel shortening and gemination of みとうもない (mitōmonai), euphonic sound change of みたくもない (mitakumonai, “don't even want to see”) (via deletion of the intermediate /k/, a regular process in Japanese).

headline: Maniau is 間 (ma, “spatial interval, temporal interval”) plus に (ni) plus 合う (au, “to match, to fit”).

sources.quote: From 間(ま) (ma, “spatial interval, temporal interval”) + に (ni, “to, at”, indirect object particle) + 合(あ)う (au, “to match, to fit”).

headline: Yakeru is from Old Japanese 焼く (yaku), in the lower bigrade pattern.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 焼く (yaku), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern. See the entry for further details.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

sources.quote: From ran (乱, disordered, confused, chaotic) + bō (暴, acting with destructive force).

headline: Toshin is 都 (to, “metropolis”) plus 心 (shin, “central part”).

sources.quote: From 都 (to, “metropolis”) + 心 (shin, “central part”).

headline: Oku is rooted in Old Japanese despite overlapping with a goon reading from Middle Chinese, and is cognate with 沖 (oki, “the open sea, offshore”).

sources.quote: Despite the apparent overlap with the modern goon reading of oku that is derived from Middle Chinese, this term is actually rooted in Old Japanese, appearing in the Man'yōshū collection of poetry dating to roughly 759 CE. Cognate with 沖 (oki, “the open sea, offshore”), originally in reference to “somewhere far removed, possibly out of sight”. While oki came to mean “far removed in the wide open → far off shore”, oku instead came to mean “far removed inside → inside, interior”.

headline: Makura is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, and has Proto-Ryukyuan cognates such as Okinawan makkwa.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *makura.
Cognates

Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *makura, whence Kikai 枕 (makka), Kunigami 枕 (makkā), Miyako 枕 (maffa), Northern Amami Ōshima 枕 (makura), Okinawan 枕 (makkwa), Okinoerabu 枕 (makura), Southern Amami Ōshima 枕 (makra), Tokunoshima 枕 (makkwa), Yaeyama 枕 (maffa), Yonaguni 枕 (magura), and Yoron 枕 (makkura).

sources.quote: From 坊(ぼう) (bō, “boy”) + や (ya, interjectory particle). Compare 婆(ばあ)や (bāya), 爺(じい)や (jīya), 姉(ねえ)や (nēya). Resemblance to English boy is coincidental.

sources.quote: From お坊(ぼう)さん (obōsan).
